data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dilemma dissolves if we treat the preference for corroborated theories as a convention or decision postulate, similar to choosing axioms, rather than a discovery of objective probability, thus preserving Popper's anti-inductivism at the cost of grounding rationality in social agreement.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the decision is arbitrary, undermining the claim of rationality.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the convention itself requires an inductive justification to be adopted.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If this leads to relativism where any decision rule is as good as another.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper explicitly frames the choice of the best-tested theory as a 'decision.' In this view, there is no logical bridge between 'survived tests' and 'should be used.' The bridge is built by a voluntary commitment to a rule of procedure: 'We decide to act as if the best-tested theory is the most reliable.' This avoids smuggling in induction because it makes no claim about the world guaranteeing the theory's success.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
